concepts.definition: The loop of write, try, judge, change one thing, try again.
concepts.example: Write v1, look at the result against the goal, add one sentence in v2.
concepts.pitfall: Saying "done" at the first attempt; a prompt does not mature until the real result has been seen.

concepts.definition: Changing only one thing in each round, so the cause of the result can be understood.
concepts.example: First adding only the format sentence, then only the role.
concepts.pitfall: Changing five things at once and not being able to tell which one worked.

concepts.definition: Writing down each prompt version, the change made and the result.
concepts.example: v1: 20 points; v2: format sentence added, 50 points.
concepts.pitfall: Deleting the old version; if things get worse, you cannot go back.

concepts.definition: The number the Workshop checker gives based on whether the parts are there; it is not a model.
concepts.example: Writing "at most 3 bullet points" fills the format and constraint boxes.
concepts.pitfall: Thinking the score is quality; the checker does not understand meaning, it looks for words and patterns.

concepts.definition: The rate of correct answers after trying the prompt with example inputs.
concepts.example: If 5 of 8 attempts are correct, 62.5 per cent.
concepts.pitfall: Drawing a conclusion from too few examples (for example 1-2).

quiz.prompt: When improving a prompt, why should you change only one thing in each round?
options: Because only this way can you understand which change the result came from
Because the model cannot read more than one change
Because the score only goes up with a single change
Because keeping a version record is not allowed
quiz.explanation: With a single change, cause and effect are visible; if it does not work, you undo it. The model can read several changes; the problem is that you cannot explain the result. On the contrary, keeping a version record is recommended.

quiz.prompt:
You tried a prompt on 8 examples and listed the results as true (correct) and false (wrong). What does the code print when it runs?

```
const sonuclar = [true, false, false, true, true, false, true, true]
const dogru = sonuclar.filter((s) => s).length
console.log(dogru / sonuclar.length * 100)
```
quiz.explanation: filter keeps only the true ones: 5 of them. length gives 8. 5 / 8 × 100 = 62.5. 37.5 is the rate of wrong answers (3 / 8); 5 is just the number of correct answers.

quiz.prompt: You tried the v1 prompt on 10 real examples: 5 correct. You tried v2 on the same 10 examples: 7 correct. By how many percentage points did the rate of correct answers go up?
quiz.explanation: v1: 5 / 10 = 50%, v2: 7 / 10 = 70%. The difference is 20 percentage points. Because you compared on the same set of examples, the cause of the result is the prompt change; if you had compared with different examples, the result would be misleading.

quiz.prompt: In the Workshop the check score went up from 50 to 80, but on a real model the answers got worse. How can this happen?
options: The checker is also a language model and it got it wrong
The checker looks at keywords; when words are added the score goes up, but it does not measure meaning or model behaviour
A real model always follows the score
quiz.explanation: The checker is rule-based, not a model. It gives points when it sees the words for the parts; instructions contradicting each other, or the answer getting worse, do not affect it. For proof you need measurement on real examples.

quiz.prompt: Going from v1 to v2, you added the role, format and constraint sentences together; success went up from 40 per cent to 80. What can you say?
options: You cannot know which of the three changes had the effect
quiz.explanation: Because three things changed together, you cannot separate the effect. Adding them one at a time, or undoing them, would show which one worked. The three changes together may have been good; but which one contributed most is unknown.
